value.body: A marine engineer runs and maintains a ship's main engines, generators, pumps and other machinery. Shipping companies and ship-management firms hire them for contracts at sea. A typical day involves engine room watches, planned maintenance, repairs and record-keeping.

items.label: Typical entry
items.value: B.Tech/B.E. Marine Engineering (4 years), or a 1-year Graduate Marine Engineering course after a Mechanical degree

items.label: Rank ladder
items.value: Engine cadet → Fourth Engineer → Third Engineer → Second Engineer → Chief Engineer
items.note: Each step needs a DG Shipping MEO certificate (Class IV up to Class I)

items.label: Indian seafarers (all ranks)
items.note: Officers and ratings, deck and engine combined
items.source: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways via PIB (as reported)

value.title: How you get in
value.body: After Class 12 with Physics, Chemistry and Maths, join a DG Shipping-approved marine engineering course (entry often through IMU-CET), or take the Graduate Marine Engineering course after a Mechanical degree. You sail as an engine cadet to build sea time, then pass the MEO Class IV exams to become an officer.

value.title: Skills you'll use
items: Operating diesel engines, boilers and auxiliary machinery
Planned maintenance and engine room records

value.title: At a glance
items: Getting a cadet berth with a company is a common hurdle after the course.
Long months at sea away from family are part of the job.
Later moves ashore include technical superintendent, surveyor and shipyard roles.
Engine rooms are hot and noisy; physical fitness matters.
